newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: BolsWessanen 1996 net seen at DFL 181 mln.
newsitem.headline: BolsWessanen 1996 net seen at DFL 181 mln.

text.p: Few surprises are expected from Dutch food and drinks group BolsWessanen's 1996 results on Thursday, with the market sticking close to the company's own forecast of a 10 percent drop in net profits over the year.
Attention will instead focus on the troubled firm's prospects for the current year and, specifically, management strategy for the future, analysts said.
Analysts polled by Reuters saw 1996 full-year net profit in a tight range of between 175 and 185 million guilders, versus 203 million in 1995, with a consensus estimate of 181 million.

"I think what could drive the share price is not these results, but announcements from management regarding the 1997 outlook and perhaps possible indications of further restructuring of the business," said David Kerstens, analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.

BolsWessanen said in August it expected net profits from ordinary operations to show a drop of 10 percent over the full year after first half net fell by 21.6 percent due to poor conditions in its cereal businesses and falling dairy margins.
It also warned of extraordinary restructuring charges of 10 to 15 million guilders in the second half.
"I think the market is waiting mainly to see what (chairman) Mac Zondervan will say about the future," Lambert Oorthuizen, analyst at Amstgeld, said.

A higher dollar and lira are expected to have been aiding the business, which has significant sales in the U.S. and Italy, in 1997 and with the shares at a 25 percent discount to the sector a good forecast could spark buying interest.
"If they are going to be positive about 1997 then we will see positive movement in the share price," Kerstens said.
"I wouldn't bet on it in view of bad experiences in the past, but you could give them the benefit of the doubt."
"My feeling is not that good for the company," Oorthuizen said. "They have said that in the near future they will come up with a new strategy, but up to now they do not have one."
Drinks firm Bols merged with food and dairy concern Wessanen in 1993, intending to use the high margins and earnings of Bols to expand in Wessanen's markets.

But the low growth potential of the group's core activities has been a major problem and it has struggled to find sizeable acquisitions in growing markets to meet a stated target of 10 percent yearly earnings growth.
Kerstens said ABN AMRO expected BolsWessanen's earnings per share to increase by around eight percent in 1997, with net results rising by around ten percent.
"But that's not very exciting since we've upgraded all our forecasts on the back of new currency views and higher growth for the market as a whole," he said.
Amstgeld's Oorthuizen warned that another failure to clarify the group's future plans could see the already-underperforming shares lagging even further behind.
"If they have no strategy at all and just say their markets are quite difficult again, the stock could well lose ground."
